posts.name: Arka Bhuiyan
posts.cooked:
Yesterday, I upgraded my Fedora Linux 39 KDE spin to the later version, Fedora Linux 40. Overall, the transition went smoothly, but I encountered a hiccup: sluggish rendering on my external monitor.

It seems this slowdown is attributable to Wayland, as I didn’t experience such issues on Plasma 5.27. However, the introduction of Plasma 6 may have altered compatibility, especially considering the NVIDIA GPU on my laptop.

To shed more light on the situation, I’ve included my system information below. Despite experimenting with the default Breeze theme, the rendering problem persists on the external monitor. Any insights or solutions would be greatly appreciated.

Operating System: Fedora Linux 40
KDE Plasma Version: 6.0.3
KDE Frameworks Version: 6.0.0
Qt Version: 6.6.2
Kernel Version: 6.8.7-300.fc40.x86_64 (64-bit)
Graphics Platform: Wayland
Processors: 12 × 11th Gen Intel® Core™ i5-11260H @ 2.60GHz
Memory: 15.3 GiB of RAM
Graphics Processor: Mesa Intel® UHD Graphics
Manufacturer: HP
Product Name: Victus by HP Laptop 16-d0xxx

I hope this information will suffice the analysis.

posts.name: Espionage724
posts.cooked:
When I last used Optimus, it was back around when NV released some newer PRIME method for rendering everything on the NVIDIA GPU at all times and doing nothing with the Intel iGPU. It sounds like your external monitor is on the NVIDIA GPU and something isn’t working right there (may be Plasma/Wayland/NVIDIA or something with the NVIDIA driver).

It’s possible with a distro upgrade you have to reinstall the GPU driver. I used to do akmods --force manually after a kernel upgrades and I’d try that. Probably wouldn’t be a bad idea to reinstall the whole graphics driver to be sure everything is in-place after the distro upgrade.

posts.name: Jeff V
posts.cooked:
Before doing a full reinstall of the driver I would look at the output of dnf list installed \*nvidia\* and post that here. Also the output of lsmod | grep nvidia.
There was a recent update to the nvidia driver with version 550.76 on rpmfusion.

If you already have that driver version and suspect the nvidia driver then a simple 3 step process should fix it

  1. dnf remove kmod-nvidia-$(uname -r)
  2. akmods --force
  3. reboot

posts.name: Jeff V
posts.cooked:
Please run lsmod | grep -E "nvidia|nouveau" and post that here.
We need to know for sure what driver is actually in use.

Without the nvidia driver it requires that graphics rendering be offloaded to the cpu which impacts the speed of everything on the laptop. Only the nvidia driver allows hardware acceleration to be used with an nvidia GPU

Check the Owners Manual on the OEM website. Sometime, they can route the port of the second monitor to the iGPU / APU depending how the machines was setup. If your GPU can only power the Monito of your Laptop, when you plug in HDMI or DisplayPort the configuration can change if it’s set up that way.

It’s confusing, but it does happen.

There seems to be some issues regarding 2nd monitors and Charging, USB-C port/HDMI.

How did you plug the 2nd in?

posts.name: Espionage724
posts.cooked:
Do cat /sys/module/nvidia_drm/parameters/modeset

If it says N, add both nvidia_drm.modeset=1, along with either nvidia_drm.modeset=1 (try first) or nvidia_drm.fbdev=1 (experimental) as kernel options: https://wiki.archlinux.org/title/NVIDIA#DRM_kernel_mode_setting

There’s some tips here too:

https://community.kde.org/Plasma/Wayland/Nvidia

posts.name: Lachlan Craig
posts.cooked:
Hi! I might’ve had the same issue with an RX580 eGPU. I fixed this by using the KWIN_DRM_DEVICES environment variable in /etc/environment.
To do this, just do sudo nano /etc/environment and add :
KWIN_DRM_DEVICES="/dev/dri/by-path/pci-0000\:03\:00.0-card:/dev/dri/by-path/pci-0000\:00\:02.0-card"
The above example is to indicate that the prioritised gpu to render the screen will be the one at the 0000:03:00.0 PCI adress (my RX580 when plugged in) and, in case that gpu is missing, it will use the one at 0000:00:02.0 which is my Intel Iris Xe. You’ll most likely have to change that by doing lspci | grep VGA which will return the correct PCI paths which you’ll have to change in the environment variable.
However, this environment variable is only detected and put in use when kwin starts , so when you login or when you do kwin --replace in your session (it will close some if not all windows and “reload the DE” ). I don’t know how it will behave on a laptop with both iGPU and dGPU however, but you should try it. Maybe you’ll just have to log out / reload kwin when plugging in you external display.
This was already a problem before KDE 6, and KDE 6 is supposed to have fixed multi-gpu configurations, which it has since you can use your external monitor in plug-and-play, but the subpar performance remains.
